claim_text: The NEET PG 2025 exam has been rescheduled to 17th August 2025, with the cut-off date for eligibility continuing to be 15th August 2025, attributed to the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS).
doctor_explanation: The claim that the NEET PG 2025 exam has been postponed to 17th August 2025 is FALSE. A fabricated notice dated 01/04/2025 has been shared on various platforms suggesting that the NEET PG 2025 exam has been postponed to 17th August 2025. This notice falsely attributes the rescheduling to the NBEMS. As of the latest official update from the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) dated 17th March 2025, the NEET PG 2025 will be held on 15th June 2025, and NBEMS has announced no rescheduling. The authentic and latest official notification from NBEMS was released on 17th March 2025, which clearly states: 'National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) shall conduct the NEET-PG 2025 on 15th June 2025 on a Computer Based Platform in Two Shifts.' The circulated notice mentioning 17th August 2025 has been officially dismissed as incorrect and should not be considered genuine. Several users in the comments section of the post on X are calling out the content as FAKE. For instance, @medicos_09 labeled it 'fake'. PIBFactCheck also conducted a fact check on X and confirmed that the notice circulated was fake. The official communication regarding the conduction of the NEET PG exam is available on the NBEMS website (https://natboard.edu.in) and supersedes any unverified claims or manipulated notices appearing online. Students are advised to disregard unofficial sources and follow the official NBEMS website for accurate updates.

claim_text: Cure to Covid-19 has been found in local fruit Sapota, commonly known as Chikoo.
doctor_explanation: The photo is clearly altered. Though the top header contains the logo of Times of India, it has no dates, location of the edition and other details that go in the header. A closer observation also shows clear discrepancy in the fonts used and alignment of the text. A quick search on The Times of India website does not show any such article in the digital version. There is no research that suggests Chikoo can cure Covid-19. No authority institutions including the World Health Organization (WHO), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), or ICMR have listed Chikoo in the available treatments for COVID-19. Like many fruits, Chikoo is loaded with dietary fibre, and vitamins A, B, and C and is also packed with antioxidants. This makes it a great addition in diet for boosting immunity. However, the fruit alone cannot cure Covid-19. Another claim suggests that eating chikoo can improve eyesight, which is false.

claim_text: Turmeric can purify blood
doctor_explanation: Dr Almas Fatma, a diabetologist in Mumbai, explains, "No herbs or natural remedy can 'purify' blood in the medical sense, like dialysis does for individuals with kidney failure. Dialysis is a medical procedure that filters waste, excess fluids, and toxins from the blood when the kidneys are no longer able to perform this function. While some herbs are believed to support liver or kidney function, they cannot replace the role of these organs or perform the complex filtration required to cleanse the blood. Healthy lifestyle habits, including proper hydration and balanced nutrition, support overall detoxification, but they don't 'purify' the blood directly." Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, says, "No, turmeric does not 'purify' your blood in the way that some traditional medicine claims. The concept of 'blood purification' is a bit ambiguous and doesn't have a precise medical definition. While turmeric is an excellent anti-inflammatory and antioxidant, there's no scientific evidence to suggest that it directly cleanses or detoxifies the blood." She further explains, "Turmeric contains an active compound called curcumin, which has been studied for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. These properties can support overall health by reducing inflammation and oxidative stress in the body, but this doesn't translate into the blood being 'purified' as some might believe." Dr Mohit Sandhu, BAMS|CAD|CAC|PGDAKS from Gurgaon says, "Turmeric might support the liver's function by reducing inflammation and providing antioxidant support, but it doesn't actively 'detox' the blood or body." Detoxification primarily happens in the liver, kidneys, and other organs, which naturally filter out toxins. Some studies show that curcumin (turmeric's active ingredient) can support liver health, which is crucial for the body's natural detoxification process. However, this support doesn't mean turmeric is removing harmful substances directly from the blood. The liver's job is to break down and remove toxins, and while turmeric may help improve liver function, it doesn't replace or accelerate this process. While turmeric is a powerful and beneficial spice with anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, the idea that it 'purifies' the blood is not scientifically supported. The body's natural detoxification mechanisms are far more capable of removing toxins than any supplement or spice. Turmeric can support these processes by promoting liver health and reducing inflammation, but it doesn't cleanse the blood directly.

claim_text: An Instagram post suggests that kalonji seeds are extremely powerful, claiming that Ayurveda refers to them as the "Black Seeds of Miracle" and that the Quran states these seeds can cure every illness except death. The post goes on to say that the seeds truly live up to the hype. In the accompanying video, it's written that kalonji can cure several health conditions, including diabetes, hair fall, thyroid problems, and more.
doctor_explanation:
## Does kalonji cure diabetes completely?
No, kalonji cannot cure diabetes. While kalonji seeds have been studied for their potential to help regulate blood sugar levels, there's no scientific evidence that they can cure diabetes and diabetes whether its type 1 or type 2 cannot be cured.
What some early research does suggest is that thymoquinone, a compound found in kalonji, might have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. These could play a small supporting role in helping the body manage blood sugar. A few small studies have modest improvements in fasting blood glucose when kalonji is taken alongside prescribed medication.
But, and this is important, kalonji is not a replacement for insulin or oral anti-diabetic drugs. The most trusted diabetes guidelines globally do not list kalonji as a treatment. Relying on it alone could lead to dangerous sugar spikes, nerve damage, or even organ failure over time.
Dr Almas Fatma, a General Physician from Navi Mumbai with qualifications in Family Medicine and Digital Health, explains that consuming kalonji seeds, whether raw, in food, or as oil, cannot cure diabetes. She stresses that diabetes is a complex metabolic condition with no known cure at present. Proper management involves a balanced diet, regular physical activity, and often medication under medical supervision. Believing in unverified claims, she warns, can be risky and may lead to delays in getting the right treatment. Consulting qualified healthcare professionals is essential for safe and effective diabetes care.
Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, a General Physician at Holy Mission Clinic in New Delhi, highlights that effectively managing diabetes demands a lifelong dedication to healthy lifestyle choices, regular physical activity, proper medical treatment, and routine blood sugar checks. He warns that depending on unproven remedies can lead to delays in essential care and increase the risk of serious health complications.

## Can kalonji stop hair fall for good?
No, kalonji cannot permanently stop hair fall. The idea that black seeds are a miracle for hair growth has gained popularity thanks to social media influencers and beauty bloggers. Some DIY hair oils now include kalonji oil, claiming it thickens hair and stops shedding.
Kalonji oil does have fatty acids and antioxidants, which may improve scalp health. There are small lab-based studies that suggest it might reduce inflammation on the scalp, which can help with certain types of hair fall, especially if it's caused by mild inflammation or dryness.
However, hair fall can have many causes, hormonal imbalances, genetics, iron deficiency, stress, thyroid issues, or autoimmune conditions. No single ingredient, including kalonji, can address all of them. If your hair fall is caused by something deeper like hypothyroidism or PCOS, rubbing oil or drinking seed water won't solve the problem. You'll need proper diagnosis and treatment.
Dr Rashi Soni, Co-founder and Consulting Dermatologist at Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, states that addressing hair fall needs a well-rounded approach involving good nutrition, proper scalp care, and medical treatment when necessary. She notes that a diet rich in protein, vitamins, and essential minerals helps nourish hair follicles and promote stronger hair. Avoiding excessive heat styling and harsh chemical products also plays a key role in protecting scalp health. For hair loss linked to hormonal issues or genetics, scientifically proven treatments like minoxidil or prescription drugs may be needed. She emphasises the importance of consulting a dermatologist for an accurate diagnosis and a treatment plan tailored to the root cause of the problem.

## Can kalonji fix thyroid problems naturally?
No, kalonji cannot treat or cure thyroid issues. Thyroid disorders, whether it's an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) or overactive one (hyperthyroidism), are complex hormonal problems. They involve the thyroid gland producing too little or too much thyroid hormone, and both conditions need careful management, usually with lifelong medication.
A handful of animal studies have explored how thymoquinone from kalonji affects the thyroid in rats, and one very small human trial suggested minor improvements in thyroid function when kalonji was used alongside standard medicine. But the evidence is too weak and inconsistent to say kalonji alone can treat the condition.
If you're experiencing fatigue, weight changes, or mood swings due to thyroid issues, self-medicating with herbs could delay proper care and make things worse.
Dr Annusuiya Gohil, an MD Scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, shares that while herbs like kalonji are valued in Ayurveda for their cooling and digestive benefits, they are not a substitute for standard thyroid medications. She emphasises that Ayurveda encourages a balanced and holistic approach, and in the case of serious thyroid conditions, it's essential to integrate traditional remedies with modern medical treatments under professional supervision.

## So, is there any safe way to use kalonji in daily life?
Yes, kalonji can be a part of a healthy diet, but not a cure. Kalonji is rich in antioxidants and may help support overall health in small ways. Using it as a spice in curries, chutneys, or teas is generally safe for most people. Just don't overdo it, large doses can irritate your stomach or interfere with medications. And always check with a doctor if you're on thyroid or diabetic medications, to avoid interactions.
The claim that drinking kalonji can cure diabetes, hair fall, and thyroid issues doesn't have any strong medical evidence. While black seeds may have mild health benefits and could complement a balanced diet, they are not magical remedies. Relying on them to treat serious health conditions could delay proper care and lead to complications.

claim_text: Drinking raisin water daily with empty stomach for 30–45 days. It helps to remove acne/pimples providing glowing skin. It works as a blood purifier.
doctor_explanation: The kidneys are essential for blood purification, filtering about half a cup of blood every minute to remove waste and excess water, which are excreted as urine. When kidney function fails, blood purification is carried out through specialized therapies outside the body — including dialysis, filtration, or adsorption. These methods act rapidly and are used in emergency situations (e.g., plasmapheresis to remove toxins), life-sustaining treatments (e.g., hemodialysis for kidney failure), and managing immune or metabolic conditions (e.g., immunoadsorption for autoimmune disorders). Dr Poojitha Byreddy, Senior Haematologist, CARE Hospitals, Hi-tech City, Hyderabad, said: 'Some people believe that drinking raisin water can clean or purify the blood in 30 to 45 days, but there is no medical proof for this. Our body already has a natural way of removing waste and toxins through the liver and kidneys. While raisins do have healthy nutrients like iron and antioxidants, raisin water alone cannot clean your blood. It is important to remember that no single food or drink can change how your blood works. Eating a balanced diet and staying healthy is more effective. Always talk to a doctor if you have any concerns about your blood.' Dr Imran Khan, Senior Consultant – Internal Medicine, CARE Hospitals, Musheerabad, Hyderabad, said: 'Raisin water might help with digestion and give your body some energy, but it will not purify your blood. The idea that a drink can clean your blood is a common myth and not backed by science. Your liver and kidneys already do that job naturally every day. Good health does not come from just one drink. It comes from eating a variety of healthy foods, drinking enough water, and staying active. If you are worried about your health or have specific problems, it is best to speak with a doctor rather than relying on home remedies.' A review published in the Journal of Nutrition and Health reported that consuming raisins, when compared to other carbohydrate-rich snacks with equal caloric value, can lead to reductions in LDL (bad) cholesterol and blood pressure, and is associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease. A study by Margaret J. Schuster et al. found that consuming raisins offers several health benefits, contributing to overall wellness and helping prevent various chronic conditions such as cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, gastrointestinal disorders, and dental caries. While raisins have some health benefits, no scientific evidence or medical consensus supports the claim that raisin water can purify, detoxify, or cleanse the blood in 30-45 days.

claim_text: We have been brainwashed into using toothpaste and it should never be used as it contains various chemicals, such as fluoride and is made by secret individuals in the lab. It further states that can hamper the brain, making it function at low levels and develop conditions, such as dementia.
doctor_explanation: Brushing your teeth is essential for maintaining good oral hygiene and promoting overall health. Toothpaste is generally recommended and should be used as a part of your daily oral hygiene routine to maintain good oral health. It removes plaque which is a sticky film of bacteria that can lead to cavities and gum disease. Brushing also freshens breath by removing food particles and bacteria to avoid bad breath. Poor oral health can cause various health problems, including heart disease, stroke, and diabetes, so regular brushing is essential. However, it's important to use it in moderation, choose toothpaste with appropriate ingredients for your needs, and brush gently to avoid damaging your teeth or gums. The choice of toothpaste can depend on your individual dental needs, such as sensitivity, cavity prevention, or gum health. Remember, it is advisable not to swallow toothpaste as it contains certain chemicals, such as fluoride. If you have any doubts or concerns about which toothpaste to use or if you should use toothpaste at all, it's best to consult with your dentist or dental hygienist for personalized guidance based on your specific oral health needs. Regarding fluoridated toothpastes: Rarely. Fluoride toothpaste strengthens tooth enamel, which can prevent cavities. It also prevents gum disease by removing plaque and bacteria that can cause inflammation and infection in the gums. It can be harmful only in a certain scenario. Many dentists recommend the topical use of fluorine because of its cariostatic effect that prevents the formation of dental caries. The Indian dental Association (IDA) website states that the topical use of fluorides is 'the most effective and economical method of protecting the teeth against decay'. Dr. Paridhi Garg, Endodontist, adds, 'Fluoride makes the tooth enamel stronger by remineralizing the lost enamel and by disrupting the cavity-causing bacteria. Fluoride can be incorporated into our teeth by adding it to our diet, drinking water and toothpaste. But in excess, fluoride can be harmful for your teeth and bones so a dentist's guidance becomes imperative'. For the body, excessive long-term exposure to fluoride can have adverse effects which include, osteoporosis, tooth decay and damage to bones, kidneys, reproductive organs, nerves and muscle. However, fluoride in low concentration maintains and solidifies bones and prevents dental caries. That being the case, fluoride is widely used in toothpaste because it prevents tooth decay. Dr. Sandeep Sharma, Dental Surgeon in Delhi, said, 'Fluoride is good for teeth because it hardens the enamel to prevent demineralization and cavities. However, the fluoride should be used in moderate amounts. Chronic and regular consumption of high levels of fluoride results in white flecks and yellow or brown areas scattered over the tooth surface.' Addressing brain harm claims: There is no credible scientific evidence to suggest that using toothpaste as directed can harm your brain. Toothpaste is specifically formulated for oral use and is not designed to have any adverse effects on the brain or neurological system when used as intended. Toothpaste is primarily composed of mild abrasives, fluoride, detergents, flavorings, and other ingredients that are safe for oral hygiene. The fluoride in toothpaste, for example, is beneficial for strengthening tooth enamel and preventing tooth decay when used properly and in appropriate quantities. The ingredients in toothpaste are not known to have any harmful neurological effects. It's important to use toothpaste in the recommended manner, which includes applying a small amount (about the size of a pea) to your toothbrush, brushing your teeth gently, and spitting out the toothpaste after brushing. Swallowing small amounts of toothpaste during brushing is generally not harmful for adults, but it should be minimized, especially in the case of young children, to avoid excessive fluoride ingestion and in case of overdosage, contact the doctor immediately. In conclusion, it is better to brush your teeth twice a day with toothpaste for at least two minutes each time. Just remember to use a gentle technique, a good quality toothbrush, and follow a consistent oral care routine to keep your teeth and gums in the best possible condition. Also, it is beneficial to visit your dentist regularly for professional cleanings and check-ups.

claim_text: Applying essential ginger oil on belly button can lead to belly drainage, resulting in weight loss
doctor_explanation: Fat can be reduced by eating a balanced diet with fiber and protein. One should also avoid alcohol, processed foods, sugar, and high-fat food items. Physical activities such as exercise, strength training, and swimming will help reduce fat. Research states that a type of belly fat called visceral fat is a significant risk factor for type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and other conditions. Hence, one must lose extra fat and keep the BMI (Body Mass Index) in proportion. Physical activities such as exercise, strength training, and swimming will help reduce fat. Secondly, there might be certain underlying medical conditions due to which one is gaining weight, such as diabetes, thyroid disease, and PCOS, to name a few. In such cases, treating the underlying condition is necessary to lose weight. Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director, Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda (ĀCĀRA), further explains this precisely from Ayurvedic perspective by stating that, 'As per Ayurveda, obesity is a condition difficult to cure. In fact, the text states bluntly that it is almost an incurable disease – na hi sthulasya bheshajam. There is no magical remedy for obesity. No single medicine, internal or external, can treat the problem. Stress management, lifestyle, and diet constitute the main approach to treatment. Medicines, either external or internal, are only supportive. The more patients comply with the comprehensive protocol, the better the results. Obesity also requires an individualized treatment protocol.' Does ginger help in weight loss? Yes. Ginger is believed to aid in weight loss, when consumed. Although, it must be used in conjunction with physical activity, dietary regulations and lifestyle modifications. It decreases inflammation, stimulates digestion, and suppresses your appetite. A meta-analysis done in 2017 says that, 'Supplementation with ginger significantly decreased body weight (BW), waist-to-hip ratio (WHR), and insulin resistance.' Gingerol, a bioactive compound in ginger has anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties which help in weight loss. A research that studied the effects of gingerol present in ginger concluded that, 'Ginger supplementation suppresses obesity induced by a high fat diet and it might be a promising adjuvant therapy for the treatment of obesity and its complications.' Please note that these studies are linked with consumption of ginger and not application of ginger on the body. What is the significance of applying oil on belly button? In Ayurveda, a method called as, 'The Pechoti method' is based on the concept that you can absorb substances like essential oils through your belly button. This includes massaging for pain relief and relaxation. It may make you feel warm from the inside and generate heat in the body but that is just because of the elements present in it. Does applying ginger oil on the belly button help in weight loss? No. There is no scientific evidence which can prove that applying ginger oil on belly button can eliminate cellulite, or subcutaneous fat, resulting in weight loss. The navel becomes closed off once the umbilical cord is detached at the time of birth. Moreover, it is based on the claim that it stimulates the pechoti gland, that sits behind the navel. But, there is no scientific evidence that this gland actually exists. It is true that applying essential oils to your skin can promote well-being, often when used in conjunction with a medical regime. Lastly, obesity is a disease, and it requires a multidimensional approach in which eliminating the underlying cause is vital.

claim_text: A YouTube short video claims that a clove of garlic a day can cure Hypertension, listing 9 diseases that can be cured by consuming a clove of garlic daily including high blood pressure, high cholesterol, heart disease, colds and flu, digestive issues, joint pain, cancer prevention, skin infections, and respiratory infections.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Manav Aggarwal, Consultant Cardiologist at Sanjeevan Hospital, explained: 'Hypertension, or high blood pressure, can have various primary and secondary causes. It can be caused by factors such as genetics, unhealthy lifestyle habits like poor diet and lack of exercise, stress, smoking, alcohol consumption, certain medications, underlying health conditions (like kidney disease or sleep apnea), and age-related changes in blood vessels.'

Dr Prem Aggarwal, Cardiologist and Chairman of Sanjeevan Hospitals, said: 'The term "cure" implies that the condition can be completely and permanently eradicated. Hypertension is a chronic condition that typically requires ongoing management, including lifestyle changes, medication, and monitoring. There are many medical studies that show the benefits of garlic on hypertension. But Garlic alone, especially just one clove per day, does not meet the medical definition of a cure for high blood pressure. This claim is false and misleading.'

The article further explains: Garlic has been used for centuries for its medicinal properties. It contains allicin, a compound thought to have vasodilative properties—meaning it can help expand blood vessels, thereby reducing blood pressure. Medical evidence shows that garlic consumption might have some BP-lowering properties. A 2020 systematic review by Kerien Reid of 12 trials and 553 hypertensive participants showed that garlic supplements lower systolic blood pressure (SBP) by an average of 8.3±1.9 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) by 5.5±1.9 mmHg, similarly to standard anti-hypertensive medications (PMC6966103). Another study by Rohner et al. in the form of a systematic review and meta-analysis suggested that garlic preparations may lower BP in hypertensive individuals, but the authors noted this evidence is not strong and a well-conducted powered trial of longer duration is needed. It is important to note that in many of the studies showing positive effects of garlic on high BP, these effects are observed with garlic supplements containing concentrated doses of active ingredients, not necessarily with a single clove of garlic. Hypertension or high blood pressure cannot be cured—it can only be managed. Garlic can potentially help manage the condition as part of a broader health strategy, but it cannot cure it alone. Hypertension can cause serious damage to the heart. Excessive blood pressure causes hardening of the arteries, decreasing blood flow and oxygen supply to the heart. It also affects the kidney, eventually resulting in kidney failure. The effect on both the heart and kidneys is life-threatening.

claim_text: An social media post/reel shows that through the application of a transdermal patch, a person lost a lot of weight. A WhatsApp number is also provided in the post to place an order.
doctor_explanation: What are transdermal patches? Transdermal patches are adhesive patches that are applied to an area of the skin. They are intended to work transdermally, i.e., the active ingredients transfer directly into the skin and bypass the digestive system. The transdermal patches used for weight loss contain a variety of ingredients, most of them being herbal, that enter the body through the skin. Some of the ingredients used in a weight loss patch are green coffee bean extract, Japanese mint or Hokuto mint, Açai berry, Garcinia cambogia, etc. The skin patches claim to act via two methods, namely, by boosting metabolism and reducing appetite. How can a person lose weight? To lose weight, a person must follow a multidisciplinary approach which includes dietary modifications, lifestyle alterations and treating any underlying medical condition, if present. Any external agent's role in losing weight lacks credible evidence. There might be certain underlying medical conditions due to which one is gaining weight, such as diabetes, thyroid disease, and PCOS, to name a few. In such cases, treating the underlying condition is necessary to lose weight. Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director, Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda (ĀCĀRA), further explains this precisely from an Ayurvedic perspective by stating that, "As per Ayurveda, obesity is a condition difficult to cure. In fact, the Ayurveda text states bluntly that it is almost an incurable disease – na hi sthulasya bheshajam. There is no magical remedy for obesity. No single medicine, internal or external, can treat the problem. Stress management, lifestyle, and diet constitute the main approach to treatment. Medicines, either external or internal, are only supportive. The more patients comply with the comprehensive protocol, the better the results. Obesity also requires an individualized treatment protocol." Are transdermal patches effective in losing weight? No. On doing a search for the scientific basis of the effectiveness of a transdermal patch, we could not find any credible evidence proving it. A single ingredient, which is transferred to the body in sporadic amounts can not have an impactful effect on body's fat and metabolism. It must be noted that there isn't substantial research which showcase that the ingredients that are present in these patches are beneficial or are effectively delivered through the bloodstream. Such patches aren't regulated by the FDA, therefore, the possible side effects and the risks associated with it are unknown. It is not clear about the quantity of certain ingredients that are in the patch and what are the risks associated with it. The Federal Trade Commission states, "Weight loss is an internal metabolic process. Nothing you wear or apply to the skin can cause substantial weight loss. So weight loss claims for patches, creams, lotions, wraps, body belts, earrings, and the like are false." In addition to these methods, we also came across a claim suggesting that inserting a capsule into the vagina can lead to weight loss. Another social media post promotes weight loss by soaking foot in water mixed foot effervescent tablets. However, these methods cannot guarantee weight loss.

claim_text: I Reversed My Vein Pain With This 1 Vitamin! Swollen legs? Bulging veins? This secret nutrient did wonders! The method includes taking Vitamin E capsules orally, applying Vitamin E oil topically on veins, and drinking turmeric with warm water to reverse vein pain, reduce bulging veins, and break clots naturally.
doctor_explanation: Dr Aseem Sharma, Director and Chief Dermatologist at Skin Saga Centre for Dermatology, Mumbai, shares that while massaging oil on the legs might offer temporary comfort, like easing a sense of heaviness or itchiness, it doesn't actually address the root cause of varicose veins. These veins usually develop due to damaged valves and weakened blood vessels. Real improvement often requires medical procedures such as sclerotherapy (where a sealing solution is injected), laser treatments, or minor surgeries. For proper care, it's best to see a vascular specialist. Dr Almas Fatma, a General Physician from Navi Mumbai with training in Family Medicine and Digital Health, explains that although varicose veins may appear like a skin issue, they're actually signs of deeper vein problems. Fortunately, treatment options have improved significantly. In the early stages, doctors usually recommend simple changes like daily walking, elevating the legs, and wearing compression stockings to improve blood circulation. But if the veins become painful, enlarged, or start affecting the skin, more targeted treatments are needed. These may include laser therapy, vein-closing injections, or small surgical procedures, all with minimal recovery time. Regarding oral Vitamin E: Vitamin E is a powerful antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative damage. However, there is no credible scientific evidence showing that oral Vitamin E supplements can treat or reverse varicose veins or improve venous circulation directly. Varicose veins occur due to weakened or damaged vein valves, leading to poor blood flow and vein bulging. This is a mechanical and circulatory issue, not caused by vitamin deficiency. While antioxidants like Vitamin E may slightly support overall blood vessel health, they cannot undo the physical changes in the veins. In fact, taking high doses (like 400 IU daily) long-term may increase the risk of bleeding, especially in people with heart conditions or those on blood thinners. Regarding topical Vitamin E: Applying Vitamin E oil directly on the skin may feel soothing for some, but it does not penetrate deeply enough to influence vein structure, blood flow, or clot formation. Some small studies have looked at Vitamin E's role in wound healing or skin health, but there's no solid evidence that topical use can reduce swelling, fix valves, or improve vascular health. Any relief may come from the massage itself and elevation of legs, which helps venous return, not the oil. Moreover, Vitamin E oil can cause skin reactions in some individuals, especially if applied daily. Regarding clots: Vitamin E has mild anticoagulant (blood-thinning) properties, but it does not "break clots." True clot-busting medications are prescribed only under medical supervision and are used in emergency settings, such as stroke or deep vein thrombosis. Encouraging people to rely on supplements for clot-related issues is risky. In fact, using Vitamin E along with turmeric (another natural blood thinner) could increase bleeding risk, especially in those on medications like aspirin or warfarin. Regarding turmeric: Turmeric contains curcumin, a compound known for its anti-inflammatory properties. While it may help reduce general inflammation in the body, there's no clinical evidence showing that drinking turmeric water treats varicose veins or venous pain. Like Vitamin E, turmeric may also thin the blood slightly. While some people use it for general wellness, it cannot reverse vein bulging or heal valves, which are physical problems that often require medical treatment. Regarding leg elevation: Raising your legs above heart level helps drain pooled blood, offering temporary relief from swelling and pain. This is a well-known recommendation in managing varicose veins. However, elevation only manages symptoms, it doesn't fix the vein damage. This trending advice oversimplifies a complex medical condition. Vitamin E and turmeric may offer general wellness benefits, but they cannot reverse vein damage or break clots. Topical use of Vitamin E oil has no proven effect on varicose veins, and relying on such tips could delay necessary treatment.

claim_text: An Instagram post claims that boiling lemon peels into a tea can 'flush out' heavy metals, cleanse the blood, and detox organs naturally.
doctor_explanation: Heavy metals do not behave like everyday waste products that can be washed out with fluids or herbal drinks. Once these metals enter the body, they bind strongly to proteins, bones, and organs such as the liver, kidneys, and brain. Drinking lemon peel tea does not break these bonds or remove stored metals. Some laboratory studies show that citrus peels contain fibre (like pectin) and plant compounds that can bind metals outside the body, under controlled conditions. However, the human digestive system is far more complex. During digestion, these compounds are broken down, absorbed, or excreted long before they could meaningfully attach to heavy metals in tissues. At present, there are no human clinical trials proving that lemon peel tea reduces heavy metal levels in blood or organs. Dr Divya Chauhan, Senior Ayurveda Researcher at Pratha Ayurveda, said 'In Ayurveda, lemon peel may support digestion and metabolism, but it is not described as a treatment for metal toxicity. Such conditions require proper assessment and intervention.' Dr Shalin Nagori, Consultant Pathologist and Industrial Physician, said 'Heavy metal detoxification requires specific chelating agents. There is no clinical evidence that foods or teas can remove metals already stored in human tissues.' Antioxidants and detoxification are often confused, but they are not the same thing. Lemon peel contains vitamin C and flavonoids, which help reduce oxidative stress, damage caused by unstable molecules in the body. This may support overall health, but it does not equate to removing heavy metals. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, says, 'Antioxidants support the body's defences, but they don't 'grab' heavy metals and carry them out. That's a misunderstanding of nutrition science.' Heavy metals cause harm through chemical toxicity and accumulation, not simply through oxidative stress. Antioxidants cannot neutralise or extract metals like lead or mercury once they are stored in the body. They may help reduce some secondary damage, but they do not solve the underlying problem. The human body relies on the liver, kidneys, and digestive system to process and eliminate waste. However, these systems are only partially effective against heavy metals. Some metals are excreted slowly, while others accumulate over time, especially with repeated exposure. When heavy metal levels become clinically significant, doctors use chelation therapy, which involves specialised medications that bind metals and help the body excrete them safely. This process is closely monitored because chelation itself carries risks. No food or drink, including lemon peel tea, works in the same way as these medical treatments. Lemon peel tea may support liver health indirectly by contributing antioxidants and encouraging fluid intake. Proper hydration and a diet rich in plant foods help the liver perform its everyday detox functions more efficiently. However, supporting normal liver function is not the same as treating heavy metal toxicity. A healthy liver cannot magically remove metals that are chemically bound within tissues. Claims suggesting otherwise oversimplify how the body works.

claim_text: Rubbing a cow's back can reduce high blood pressure medication dosage from 20 mg to 10 mg within 10 days, and lying down where a cow sits and cleaning the cowshed area can cure cancer.
doctor_explanation:
Dr. Prem Aggarwal MBBS, MD (Medicine), DNB Cardiology, Director, Sanjeevan Hospital, Daryaganj, Delhi said: 'Rubbing a cow's back cannot reduce the dosage of high blood pressure from 20 mg to 10 mg; this claim is not just false and frankly, quite absurd. Hypertension is a serious medical condition that requires proper medical management. It involves lifestyle changes, regular monitoring, and prescribed medications to control blood pressure levels. Ignoring medical advice and resorting to unproven remedies can lead to serious health risks, including heart attack and stroke. Promoting such baseless claims can be harmful and should not be supported. Always seek evidence-based treatment and consult your doctor for proper medical guidance.'

Prof. Dr. Somashekhar S P, Lead Consultant - Surgical & Gynaecological Oncology & Robotic Surgeon, Aster CMI Hospital, Bangalore said: 'This statement, however, has no basis in scientific fact and has been widely condemned by medical professionals. Cancer is a complex disease that arises from the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells, and its treatment requires a combination of well-established medical therapies, such as surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation. There is no scientific evidence to support the idea that cleaning a cowshed or spending time in such an environment could cure cancer. In fact, such baseless claims can put patients at risk by encouraging them to forgo proven treatments in favor of unfounded, potentially harmful alternatives. Suggesting that something as unrelated as cleaning a cowshed could cure cancer is not just misleading—it's dangerous. The problem is that such claims concern a broader challenge involving the spread of health misinformation, particularly in rural communities where quality healthcare and trustworthy information can be scarce. The minister's suggestion also highlights the growing trend of politicians and public figures offering unverified health advice, often under the guise of traditional wisdom. While traditional practices can offer cultural value and sometimes even complementary health benefits, they should never be presented as substitutes for scientifically validated medical treatments, especially when it comes to diseases as serious as cancer. The consequences of such remarks are potentially far-reaching. Patients who believe in these myths might delay or even abandon life-saving treatments, choosing instead to rely on practices that are at best ineffective and at worst harmful. Public figures must exercise responsibility when discussing health issues, particularly when the well-being of vulnerable individuals is at stake.'

The article further states: High blood pressure (hypertension) according to WHO is when blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg or higher. It can be controlled with lifestyle modifications, diet, and medications, but there is no cure. The American Heart Association notes: 'While there is no cure for high blood pressure, it is important for patients to take steps that matter, such as making effective lifestyle changes and taking BP-lowering medications as prescribed by their physicians.' Regarding cancer, WHO defines it as a large group of diseases where abnormal cells grow uncontrollably and can metastasize. Cancer is the second leading cause of death globally, accounting for an estimated 9.6 million deaths (1 in 6 deaths) in 2018. The American Cancer Society states: 'Whether a person's cancer can be cured depends on the type and stage of the cancer, the type of treatment they can get, and other factors. Some cancers are more likely to be cured than others. But each cancer needs to be treated differently. There isn't one cure for cancer.' Cancer treatment encompasses chemotherapy, hormone therapy, hyperthermia, immunotherapy, photodynamic therapy, radiation therapy, stem cell transplants, surgery, and targeted therapy — all evidence-based medical approaches. There is no scientific evidence or medical consensus that rubbing a cow's back reduces high blood pressure medication or that lying in a cow's resting spot cures cancer.

doctor_explanation: The FDA has approved the antiviral drug Veklury (remdesivir) for adults and certain pediatric patients with COVID-19 who are sick enough to need hospitalization. The FDA has issued Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) for several monoclonal antibody treatments for COVID-19 for the treatment, and in some cases prevention (prophylaxis), of COVID-19 in adults and pediatric patients. claim_text: Women should avoid taking baths during the first three days of their periods because it lowers body temperature, disrupts natural blood flow, and causes tiredness.
doctor_explanation: Bathing during periods does not cause harmful body temperature changes. Taking a bath, whether warm or cool, can cause a small and temporary rise in skin and core temperature, especially after a hot bath (but this is with long baths and not usual short showers). However, the body's natural temperature regulation keeps this change under control and prevents any danger. Menstruating women do not become dangerously cold or disturb their cycle simply by bathing. In fact, warm baths are often recommended to ease menstrual cramps and relax muscles. Dr P. Ram Manohar, Research Director at Amrita School of Ayurveda, says, 'There are no specific references in Ayurvedic texts advising against bathing or washing hair during menstruation. The idea that bathing can cause harmful body temperature changes likely stems from cultural practices, not from medical or Ayurvedic principles. Historically, challenges like limited access to clean water and sanitary products may have influenced these customs. However, there is no evidence in Ayurveda to suggest that bathing during menstruation has any harmful impact on body temperature. In fact, a warm bath can help relax the body and alleviate menstrual discomfort.' Dr Akanksha Tripathi, Senior Gynaecologist and Laparoscopic Surgeon at Paras Hospital, Udaipur, explains, 'There is no medical reason to avoid bathing during your period. In fact, maintaining your usual hygiene routine, including bathing, is important for overall health. While external temperatures may cause slight shifts in body temperature, they do not have a significant impact on menstruation or cause harmful changes to body temperature. Many women find that a warm shower can help them feel refreshed and even ease some of the discomforts associated with menstruation. The belief that bathing or washing hair during periods can cause harm is mostly due to cultural myths, not medical or scientific evidence.' Regarding blood flow: bathing does not negatively affect menstrual blood flow. Menstrual flow is controlled by the shedding of the uterine lining and hormonal activity, not by external temperature changes. While external temperatures may cause slight changes in body temperature, they don't significantly affect menstrual flow or cycle length. In fact, warm water can help relax the uterus and may even promote smoother blood flow, making periods more comfortable. There is no medical basis for the idea that bathing blocks or disrupts menstruation. Avoiding bathing during menstruation can lead to poor hygiene and increase the risk of reproductive tract infections. Dr Sumedha Gupta, Ayurveda Practitioner from New Delhi, explains, 'In Ayurveda, there is no restriction against bathing during menstruation, and traditional Ayurvedic texts do not support this idea. These beliefs likely stem from cultural customs rather than Ayurvedic principles. Bathing, especially in warm water, is actually beneficial for overall well-being during your period. It helps soothe the body and alleviate discomfort. Ayurveda encourages balance and self-care, and there is no evidence to suggest that bathing during menstruation causes harmful changes to body temperature. Women should feel empowered to prioritise their hygiene and comfort without being constrained by outdated practices.' Regarding tiredness: Taking a hot bath can cause mild relaxation, which may leave someone feeling a bit drowsy or calm afterward. This effect is similar to the relaxation experienced after a spa or sauna session and is very different from feeling tired due to 'changing the body's temperature.' Some people may confuse this relaxation with tiredness. It is not harmful and does not negatively impact menstruation. About waiting till fourth day: There is no scientific reason to delay bathing until the fourth day. Maintaining good hygiene throughout menstruation is crucial. UNESCO stresses the importance of washing the body and hair during periods for overall health. Cold water has no negative effect on your health or menstrual cycle, and bathing can help you feel refreshed and clean. Regular bathing not only keeps the body clean but also reduces the risk of infections and increases comfort. Skipping baths for several days can lead to discomfort, body odour, and may increase the risk of skin irritations. No scientific or medical guidelines recommend avoiding baths during menstruation. Dr Muskan Thakur, Ayurveda Consultant from Indore, said, 'During menstruation, cleanliness is essential, and proper care of the body, including bathing, plays an important role. I generally recommend to avoid exposure to cold water or practices that may stress the body. Bathing in lukewarm or mildly warm water is ideal. While excessive bathing or prolonged exposure to water, especially in the first few days when menstrual flow is heavier, should be avoided to maintain warmth and prevent a Vata imbalance, there is no advice in Ayurvedic texts suggesting waiting until the fourth day to bathe. Ayurveda encourages gentle self-care, and bathing with warm water is usually acceptable during menstruation. However, cold water and excessive exposure should be avoided. Ayurveda also values individual constitution and daily routines, so it's important to listen to your body. If discomfort or coldness is felt, it's better to choose warm, soothing baths instead of cold ones.'

claim_text: A Facebook post claims that onion and beetroot can cure piles in 7 days, even in people who have had the condition for many years.
doctor_explanation:
Do onion and beetroot actually cure piles within a week? No. Piles are swollen and inflamed blood vessels in or around the anus. They develop due to pressure most commonly from chronic constipation, straining during bowel movements, pregnancy, obesity, or sitting on the toilet for long periods. Because piles are a structural problem involving veins, they do not simply disappear because of one or two foods. In mild cases, symptoms like itching, discomfort, or slight bleeding may reduce within a few days if straining stops and stools become softer. However, this improvement is often mistaken for a "cure." Medically speaking, symptom relief is not the same as healing the underlying swollen veins. A guaranteed seven-day cure, especially from kitchen ingredients alone, is unrealistic.

Can onion and beetroot reduce piles by improving digestion? Partially, yes, but indirectly. Onion and beetroot contain dietary fibre, which helps add bulk to stools and supports smoother bowel movements. Softer stools mean less straining, and less straining reduces irritation of haemorrhoids. However, the fibre content of these vegetables alone is not high enough to treat constipation if the rest of the diet is poor. A single beetroot or a small serving of onion cannot compensate for an overall low-fibre diet, inadequate water intake, or poor toilet habits. Their benefit comes only when they are part of a broader pattern of eating fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and pulses regularly. So while onion and beetroot may support bowel health, they do not directly treat piles.

Do onion or beetroot have properties that shrink haemorrhoids? No. You may hear claims that onion is "anti-inflammatory" or beetroot "improves blood flow," and while these ideas come from nutrition research, they are often taken out of context. Onions contain plant compounds such as quercetin, and beetroot contains betalains and nitrates. These compounds have been studied for general anti-inflammatory or cardiovascular effects, not for curing haemorrhoids. There are no clinical trials showing that eating onion or beetroot reduces the size of piles, stops bleeding, or repairs damaged rectal veins. In medicine, when natural substances help haemorrhoids, they are usually studied in specific doses and forms (for example, certain flavonoid supplements), not as everyday vegetables promoted as miracle cures.

Why does the "7-day cure" idea sound believable to many people? Because symptoms can fluctuate. Piles often behave unpredictably. A painful flare-up may calm down within days if constipation eases or if irritation reduces. When this happens after someone starts a home remedy, the improvement is wrongly credited to that remedy. This creates a powerful illusion: "I ate onion and beetroot and felt better in a week." In reality, the improvement likely came from reduced straining, better hydration, or simply the natural settling of inflammation, not from the foods themselves. Social media and home-remedy posts often rely on personal stories rather than medical evidence, making the claim sound convincing but unreliable.

Dr Almas Fatma, a General Physician based in Navi Mumbai with in Family Medicine, and a PG degree in Digital Health, shares her expert perspective on this claim. She explains that natural approaches such as dietary modifications may help ease symptoms in mild cases of piles, but they are not sufficient for treating severe conditions like grade 4 piles, which are often painful and debilitating. She notes that while natural remedies can help soothe inflammation and support bowel regularity, grade 4 piles involve prolapsed haemorrhoids that cannot be pushed back manually, making medical or surgical intervention necessary. In such cases, treatments like rubber band ligation, sclerotherapy, or haemorrhoidectomy are far more effective, as they address the underlying cause and reduce the risk of complications. Dr Fatma further emphasises that although natural remedies may provide temporary symptom relief, they cannot replace proven medical treatments. In summary, she highlights that natural remedies can play a supportive role alongside medical care, but they should not be relied upon as a standalone solution, particularly in advanced cases such as grade 4 piles.

What actually helps piles improve within days to weeks? Evidence-based self-care does. Most mild to moderate piles improve when pressure on the veins is reduced and the area is allowed to heal.

Can diet alone permanently cure piles? No. Diet is important, but it is only one part of management. Even people who eat well can develop piles if they strain, lift heavy weights incorrectly, sit for long hours, or have repeated bouts of constipation or diarrhoea. Long-term control depends on consistent habits, regular bowel movements, balanced meals, physical activity, and proper toilet posture. In some cases, medical procedures are needed when piles do not respond to lifestyle changes.

Can home remedies replace medical treatment? Home remedies may help relieve mild discomfort, but they cannot cure piles or replace proper medical care. Beetroot and onion may offer temporary digestive relief, but they do not treat the underlying problem. In mild cases, piles may improve with dietary changes, increased fibre intake, and healthier toilet habits. However, if symptoms are persistent, painful, or worsening, relying only on home remedies can delay treatment and make the condition more serious.

Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, General Physician at Holy Mission Clinic, New Delhi, explains that while home remedies may provide short-term comfort, they are not a substitute for medical treatment. He stresses that piles which bleed, cause pain, or keep recurring need proper evaluation and diagnosis. Depending solely on herbal drinks or kitchen spices may allow the condition to progress. Doctors encourage healthy lifestyle practices, but also emphasise recognising when professional medical help is necessary.

claim_text: An individual may only need to visit a therapist once in order to receive gender-affirming care.
doctor_explanation:
Gender affirmation care is a crucial aspect of healthcare that aims to support transgender individuals in aligning with their gender identity. It addresses the health disparities faced by LGBTQIA+ individuals through a comprehensive approach that includes medical, psychological, and social interventions. These interventions may involve hormone therapy and mental health support. It is important to note that gender-affirming care goes beyond medical treatments and encompasses respecting an individual's chosen name and pronouns, creating a safe and inclusive healthcare environment, and providing support for fertility preservation when necessary. Gender affirmation care is essential for creating a more equitable healthcare system by promoting inclusivity, reducing disparities, and improving the well-being of transgender individuals. 

Therapists play a critical role in gender affirmation care. They provide mental health support and facilitate the gender affirmation process, helping establish a safe, comfortable, and tailored therapeutic environment that builds trust and understanding between the therapist and the patient. Therapists also address ethical considerations when it comes to gender-affirming care, which is particularly important when working with transgender and gender-nonconforming (TGNC) youth. This ensures that care is provided in an affirmative and non-discriminatory manner.

Gender-affirming therapy does NOT necessitate just one session. Gender affirmation care is a multifaceted and continuous process that goes beyond a single therapy session. It covers a range of healthcare measures aimed at assisting transgender individuals in living and being recognised in accordance with their gender identity and expression. By offering mental health assistance, addressing emotional wellbeing, and helping people through their gender journey, therapists play a critical part in gender affirmation care. The phase of gender affirmation frequently goes through various stages and might involve hormone therapy, gender-affirming surgery, and social transformation. These actions usually take place over time and necessitate ongoing monitoring and support from healthcare professionals, including therapists. Transgender and gender-nonconforming individuals require ongoing, patient-centred management due to the unique challenges they face.

Dr. Sameer Kalani, Senior Consultant Psychiatrist, HOD Mental Health and Behavioural Sciences, Fortis Memorial and Research Institute, Gurugram, stated: Supporting people who are looking for gender affirmation is a rigorous and continuing process that involves many different forms of healthcare. It is imperative to have a comprehensive and ongoing strategy in order to adequately accompany people on their gender affirmation journey. Hence, it could take more than one appointment to improve their general well-being and affirm their gender identification.

Dr. Manisha Gaur, psychologist, stated: Gender affirmation care involves multiple healthcare elements that call for an ongoing and comprehensive approach. Therapists are essential in supporting individuals throughout their gender affirmation journeys, as it is not a one-time event. The ultimate goal is to improve individuals' overall well-being and validate their gender identity, which requires an ongoing and evolving process.

Regarding safety: Access to gender-affirming care (also known as transition-related care) is an essential aspect of healthcare for individuals who identify as transgender, regardless of their age or gender. A comprehensive range of services including mental health care, medical care, and social affirmation are included. Eligibility and timing for gender-affirming care are determined by evidence-based guidelines. Gender-affirming care is provided using appropriate, scientifically proven approaches, with healthcare providers closely collaborating with patients, parents, and other healthcare experts to analyse individual requirements and ensure safety and efficacy. Dr. Manisha Gaur emphasised that evidence-based access to gender-affirming care includes mental health, medical, and social services adhering to evidence-based standards, using scientifically supported methods appropriate for the patient, and that health professionals should collaborate with patients and their parents to guarantee care is secure and efficient.

claim_text: Ginger, honey, garlic, turmeric, cayenne, onion, lime, black pepper, apple cider vinegar, and pineapple are Nature's amoxicillin.
doctor_explanation: Dr. Juhi Singla, MD (Pharmacologist), SGT UNIVERSITY Gurgaon and MBBS, Era's Lucknow Medical College said: "Amoxicillin is a penicillin-based antibiotic commonly prescribed to treat various bacterial infections, including respiratory infections, ear infections, sinusitis, skin infections, and certain urinary tract infections. It works by interfering with the bacteria's cell wall formation, leading to the destruction of the bacteria. While ingredients like ginger, honey, garlic, turmeric, cayenne, onion, lime, black pepper, apple cider vinegar, and pineapple have potential health benefits—such as boosting immunity and reducing inflammation—they cannot be natural amoxicillin. These natural remedies may support overall health but lack the antibiotic properties needed to combat specific bacterial infections. Relying solely on such natural remedies for treating bacterial infections can cause worsening of symptoms and delay necessary medical treatment, potentially leading to complications. Always seek proper treatment from doctors for accurate diagnosis and treatment." Dr. Sachin Choudhary, MBBS, MS (General Surgery), Army College of Medical Sciences further added: "Ginger, honey, garlic, turmeric, and black pepper exhibit some antibacterial properties, other ingredients like cayenne, onion, lime, apple cider vinegar, and pineapple do not. However, tagging these natural ingredients as nature's amoxicillins is incorrect. While ingredients like ginger, honey, garlic, turmeric, and black pepper have some antibacterial properties, equating their effects to antibiotics like amoxicillin is not appropriate and should not be promoted. Amoxicillin is an effective, clinically tested antibiotic specifically designed to target and kill bacteria, ensuring complete eradication. Relying solely on natural remedies instead of prescribed antibiotics can lead to worsening infections and complications. Always consult a doctor for appropriate diagnosis and treatment of the disease." The article also provides detailed evidence: A study in Food and Chemical Toxicology found ginger exhibits immunomodulatory, antioxidant, antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, anti-hyperglycemic, anti-lipidemic, and anti-emetic properties. A study by Manisha Deb Mandal et al. found honey's antibacterial effects, ability to maintain a moist wound environment, and high viscosity create a protective barrier against infection; the antimicrobial activity is primarily due to enzymatic production of hydrogen peroxide. Serge Ankri et al. revealed that allicin in garlic possesses extensive antimicrobial and antibacterial properties effective against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, fungi, and intestinal protozoa, with antiviral capabilities. A study by Bharat B. Aggarwal et al. observed that curcumin in turmeric possesses antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antiviral, antibacterial, and antifungal properties. A systematic review by Heerasing Takooree et al. found black pepper (Piper nigrum) demonstrates antibacterial, antimicrobial, antioxidant, antidiabetic, and hypolipidemic effects. Bobak J. Akhavan et al. noted amoxicillin is an FDA-approved beta-lactam aminopenicillin antibiotic indicated for ear, nose, and throat infections, Helicobacter pylori eradication, lower respiratory and urinary tract infections, acute bacterial sinusitis, and skin and soft tissue infections. Critically, while ginger, honey, garlic, turmeric, and black pepper have recognized antibacterial properties, cayenne, lime, onion, apple cider vinegar, and pineapple lack scientific evidence of antibacterial effects equivalent to amoxicillin. There is no scientific evidence or medical consensus that these natural ingredients have the same effect, potency, or purpose as antibiotic amoxicillin.

claim_text: In a video posted on Facebook, a man says, "I got a call from an animal veterinarian in western Oklahoma, who is a college friend and a family friend. He told me this crazy story about a scientist who has been doing cancer research on mice. She had hundreds of mice, and some had cancer all over the body. Her mice population was down within intestinal parasites and she had no choice but to save her research. She gave all of her mice fenbendazole. If you go to any zoo in the world, they bring in fenbendazole by a truckload front-end loader, head-high piles in bays because they give them to every single animal. And she did, and unfortunately or fortunately for all of us, she she accidentally killed all the cancer."
doctor_explanation: Fenbendazole is a broad-spectrum anthelmintic medication, which means it is effective against a wide range of parasitic worms. It is commonly used to treat and prevent intestinal parasites in animals, including dogs, cats, horses, and livestock. Fenbendazole works by disrupting the energy metabolism of parasites, specifically by inhibiting the formation of microtubules, which are essential for cell division and nutrient uptake. As a result, the parasites are unable to survive and eventually die. Can Fenbendazole cure cancer? No. Fenbendazole is a broad-spectrum antiparasitic medication primarily used to treat parasitic worm infections in animals. While some preliminary research has shown potential anti-cancer properties of fenbendazole in laboratory settings, there is currently no conclusive evidence from rigorous clinical trials to support the claim that fenbendazole can cure cancer in humans. The existing evidence is limited to in vitro (test tube) and animal studies, which have shown that fenbendazole can inhibit the growth of certain types of cancer cells. However, these findings have not been translated into effective treatments for cancer in humans. Furthermore, another research has concluded that it has no value in cancer therapy. Dr P. Rammanohar, Research Director, Amrita School of Ayurveda, highlights this by stating, "Cancer is not a single disease, and there is no remedy for cancer. Different types of cancer are treated with different procedures of chemotherapy. One drug does not work across all cancers." Moreover, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not approved fenbendazole for the treatment of cancer. Using fenbendazole for cancer treatment is considered an off-label use, meaning it is not approved for that specific purpose. Cancer treatment depends on various factors, including the type and stage of cancer. It often involves a combination of treatments such as surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. These treatments have been extensively researched and proven effective in managing and sometimes curing certain types of cancer. Shivashankar T., Chief Clinical Nutritionist and Dietician at Tata Memorial Cancer Hospital, Mumbai further informs that a good diet is important in cancer treatment. He further explains that "A healthy diet plays an important role in supporting overall health and well-being during cancer treatment. A diet high in good protein and no simple carbohydrates as well as inflammatory proteins can be beneficial for the cancer patients. However, this diet advice needs to be altered for every patient according to the requirements of their body." Our research further shows that cancer treatment typically involves a multidisciplinary approach, including medical interventions like chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, and targeted therapies. It is important to note that self-treating with fenbendazole for cancer can be dangerous. Fenbendazole can have side effects, including liver damage, and may interact with other medications. It is crucial to consult with a healthcare professional before considering any off-label use of fenbendazole or any other medication. Currently, there is no definitive evidence to support the claim that fenbendazole can cure cancer in humans. More rigorous clinical trials are needed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of fenbendazole for cancer treatment.

claim_text: "Very odd that Covid barely "mutated" for a year but once the vaccines rolled out, suddenly a whole Greek alphabet of variants appeared," tweeted George Papadopoulos, ex-aide to former President Donald Trump.
doctor_explanation: No. While the world has become more knowledgeable about the minor aspects of the novel Coronavirus due to continuous research, media coverage, and raising public awareness, the Coronavirus had started mutating much before the vaccines were invented. The news about Coronavirus starting to mutate started appearing on media by July 2020. In June 2020, China approved the CanSino vaccine for limited use in the military. In August 2020, Russia announced the approval of its Sputnik V vaccine for emergency use. But both these vaccines had limited availability. The actual launch of the vaccine can be dated to December 2020 when the US FDA granted an emergency use authorization to Pfizer–BioNTech and the Moderna vaccine. By December 2020, scientists had discovered multiple variants in many parts of the world including the Spanish variant, South African variant, Brazilian variant, etc. In fact, by the 3rd week of December 2020, World Health Organization (WHO) had named the Alpha and Beta variant. A Reuter's graphics representation that tracks the evolution of Coronavirus across 2020 will show that at least 7 strands were known to scientists before the launch of the Pfizer–BioNTech vaccine. The CDC also in a briefing in January 2021 listed down all variants that were discovered in 2020. So, it is wrong to say that the Covid virus barely mutated for a year and the new variants appeared only after the vaccines are invented. Scientists believe the mutations in the virus is quite normal. When cells replicate, the DNA sequence in them sometimes undergoes changes. These are majorly copying errors. In humans, cells have mechanisms to proofread the genome and also mechanisms to repair a sequence if an error is detected. Viruses lack that and hence they mutate faster. A virus with one or several new mutations is referred to as a "variant" of the original virus. Not always. Many times, the copying error can make the virus weaker. But sometimes, the error proves to be beneficial for the virus by making it stronger and more capable to bind with the host. If a mutation provides a survival advantage, then that mutated version becomes the dominant strain. Most of the time, scientists focus more on studying the dominant strain, and common people are also made aware of it but that does not mean that the virus only mutates to a stronger strain.

claim_text: Kidney stones can be removed in just 8 days using a home remedy of boiling one spoon each of Saunf (fennel), Ajwain (carom seeds), and Jeera (cumin) in a cup of water for 5–10 minutes, straining and taking on an empty stomach every morning, with a 100% guarantee of success.
doctor_explanation: There is no scientific proof that this mixture can dissolve kidney stones. Fennel (saunf), carom seeds (ajwain), and cumin (jeera) are often used in home remedies for digestion or bloating. Some also believe they may support urine flow. But no strong medical evidence shows that this mix can break down kidney stones. A 2023 animal study found that fennel seeds and their sprouts helped protect rat kidneys from chemical damage. The sprouted seeds had stronger antioxidant effects and improved kidney function. However, these were high doses tested in rats, not humans, and not directly for kidney stones. Furthermore, a 2024 lab study on cumin showed that its extract may help slow the growth of calcium oxalate crystals (the most common type of kidney stones). It also showed some kidney-protective effects in test tubes. But again, this was not tested in humans or as a stone treatment. Ajwain, though used in traditional medicine, did not show strong results for kidney stone treatment in a 2014 study. This mix may support general health, but there is no medical proof that it can dissolve kidney stones. Similarly, there are other home remedies that make even more exaggerated claims, such as lemon, holy basil, and coconut water curing kidney stones in a day. But this is false. How quickly a kidney stone passes depends on its size and where it is in the urinary tract. Very small stones (less than 5 mm) may pass naturally over days or even weeks. But larger stones often need medical help. There is no evidence that this drink speeds up the process. Expecting it to work in exactly 8 days is not realistic. There is no such thing as a 100% guaranteed cure or treatment for kidney stones, especially not from a home remedy. Every case is different, and even clinically proven medical treatments can't promise exact results. Claiming that this drink works for everyone in just 8 days is not only inaccurate, it's also misleading. Dr Sharad Malhotra, HOD Gastroenterology Hepatology & Therapeutic Endoscopy, Aakash Healthcare, New Delhi, told THIP Media that while certain spices may benefit digestion or urinary health, they should not be treated as cures. 'Home remedies like fennel, carom, and cumin may help improve digestion or urine flow to some extent. But there's no strong evidence that they can treat or dissolve kidney stones. People should avoid using these remedies as a substitute for proper medical care,' he said. Dr Ganesh Srinivasa Prasad P, Consultant Nephrologist at Narayana Health City, Bengaluru, also spoke to THIP Media. He explained that kidney stones are common in tropical countries due to dehydration and said that no home remedy can prevent or cure all cases. 'Reducing risk involves staying well hydrated, limiting salt, maintaining a healthy weight, eating calcium-rich foods, and avoiding high-oxalate foods. For uric acid stones, cutting down on red meat, sugar, refined carbs, alcohol, and smoking may help manage the risk,' he added.

claim_text: Bill Gates discusses using vaccines to control the global population, and this video was 'utterly scrubbed from the internet,' including its original TED Talk source. The post urges viewers to save the video and implies that authorities removed it to suppress the truth.
doctor_explanation:
The claim that Bill Gates' video discussing vaccines and population control is no longer accessible online is false. The 2010 TED Talk by Bill Gates in which he discusses population growth and vaccines is still available. Both the TED website and YouTube host the video, which millions have viewed over the years. These claims about the video's removal are incorrect. The talk remains public and easy to find, countering any notion of suppression.

Social media posts have widely misunderstood and taken Gates' statement out of context. In his talk, Gates discusses reducing carbon emissions and highlights the importance of slowing population growth to achieve net-zero emissions. His comment about reducing population growth by '10 to 15 percent' refers to improving global health and reducing child mortality rates. The talk does not specifically suggest reducing the existing population. Improving healthcare through vaccines and medical services means more children survive, leading parents to have fewer children. Families tend to choose smaller families when confident that their children will reach adulthood, which helps slow population growth over time.

The claim that Gates wants to harm people or forcibly reduce the population is misleading. The video shared on social media splices his words with footage from an anti-vaccine documentary called Died Suddenly. Anti-vaccine narratives distorted the original message to promote false claims. In a 2022 interview, Gates addressed this misinterpretation, explaining that improved health systems and higher child survival rates naturally lead to lower birth rates. As mortality rates drop and families become more confident in their children's survival, parents opt for smaller families, which slows population growth.

Initially, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation focused on family planning through contraception in poorer countries to manage high birth rates. They observed that as healthcare and vaccination programmes improved child survival rates, families naturally had fewer children. This shift led the foundation to prioritise health and vaccination initiatives as a means to improve living conditions, reduce child mortality, and stabilise population growth. Gates has reiterated in a 2011 Forbes interview and a 2018 YouTube video that reducing child mortality through better healthcare results in smaller families and sustainable population growth.

Despite his significant contributions to global health initiatives, Bill Gates has been the target of various conspiracy theories. Related false claims debunked include: Bill Gates invented a wireless birth control microchip (false); Bill Gates inserted HIV into Mpox vaccines (false); Bill Gates planned the COVID-19 pandemic (false).

claim_text: According to an Instagram post, keeping potatoes (aloo) and onions (pyaaj) together can be extremely harmful and even kill a child. The video shows a child having a seizure and claims the child died because these vegetables were stored together. It says this is not a rumour but a scientific fact. The post claims onions release a chemical that makes potatoes sprout early, leading to the formation of toxic substances called solanine and chaconine. It warns that these can make the entire family sick, causing symptoms like stomach pain, vomiting, nausea, weakness, diarrhoea, fever, headache, breathlessness, coma, or even death. The video also claims that this is often the hidden reason behind sudden deaths in children.
doctor_explanation: Can onions really make potatoes toxic? No, onions don't make potatoes toxic. It's true that storing onions and potatoes together can lead to faster spoilage, but not because onions release any toxic chemical. Both vegetables release moisture and gases that encourage each other to sprout or rot more quickly. However, this is about food quality and shelf life—not toxicity. The claim that onions trigger a chemical reaction that makes potatoes harmful is untrue. No research supports this. Do sprouted potatoes contain harmful substances? Yes, but only if eaten in large amounts or when clearly spoiled. Sprouted potatoes can contain natural chemicals called glycoalkaloids—mainly solanine and chaconine. These are part of the plant's defence system. In high amounts, they can cause mild poisoning. Symptoms may include stomach pain, vomiting, or diarrhoea. But the risk of serious illness or death from eating a small amount at home is extremely low. In 2022, a case report from Saudi Arabia described an 11-year-old boy who became sick after eating raw, sprouted potatoes. He had stomach pain, vomiting, and later developed slow heart rate and breathing issues. Doctors suspected solanine poisoning. The boy was treated in hospital and made a full recovery. The report did not mention onions or say that storing onions with potatoes caused the problem. It also said that solanine poisoning is rare and usually happens only when a large amount is eaten. Shruti K Bhardwaj, Chief Clinical Nutritionist at Zydus Hospital, Ahmedabad, explains, 'Yes, sprouted or green potatoes can develop natural compounds called glycoalkaloids, mainly solanine, which are the plant's way of defending itself. These chemicals are found in higher amounts when potatoes are exposed to light, stored for too long, or begin to sprout. If eaten in large quantities, they can irritate the stomach and, in rare cases, cause more serious symptoms. But the key thing to remember is this: the average person isn't likely to get sick from eating one or two sprouted potatoes by mistake. Just look out for green skin or deep sprouts, and if in doubt, throw it out. It's more about food quality and taste than a serious health hazard in everyday situations.' If a potato has green patches or deep sprouts, it's safest to throw it away. But keeping it near onions won't make it toxic. Can solanine poisoning kill a child? Extremely unlikely, especially from household vegetables. Severe solanine poisoning is very rare. For it to become deadly, a child would need to eat a large quantity of highly spoiled or green potatoes. The idea that one or two sprouted potatoes—caused by storing them near onions—could kill a child is scientifically baseless. The symptoms shown in the video, like seizures or coma, are not typical of common food spoilage. Is the video showing a real cause-effect situation? No, the video is misleading with unrelated visuals. The video shows a child having a seizure and connects it to storing onions and potatoes together. However, seizures in children can be due to many medical conditions, like epilepsy, high fever, or infections. There is no evidence that food spoilage which arises due to co-storage of vegetables can lead to such a reaction. The video uses fear tactics and emotional manipulation without any scientific backing. Is there any merit to keeping onions and potatoes apart? Yes, but only to reduce spoilage—not for safety reasons. Onions and potatoes should ideally be stored separately. Onions prefer dry, ventilated conditions. Potatoes last longer in cool, dark places. Storing them together may make them spoil faster, but it won't create harmful toxins. It's more about reducing food waste, not preventing illness. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, states, 'Yes, there's good reason to store onions and potatoes separately. Onions naturally release ethylene gas, which can speed up sprouting and spoilage in potatoes.
