While home remedies do not prevent kidney stones, reducing risk involves staying hydrated, cutting salt, maintaining a healthy weight, eating calcium-rich foods, and avoiding high-oxalate foods. For uric acid stones, limiting meat, sugar, carbs, alcohol, and smoking can help manage the risk. Regarding apple cider vinegar: Some studies believe that the acidity of vinegar can help 'dissolve' kidney stones, but there are no studies that specifically talk about apple cider vinegar dissolving stones. Shruti K Bhardwaj, Chief Clinical Nutritionist at Zydus Hospital, Ahmedabad, advises: 'To reduce the risk of gallstones, avoid very low-calorie diets and prioritise a balanced diet with healthy fats. Keeping a stable, healthy weight is crucial. It is also important to seek guidance from qualified professionals who provide evidence-based information, ensuring you follow trustworthy health practices.' The article notes that another post claiming boiling muskmelon peel in water can dissolve gallstones in 30 minutes is completely false. Conclusion: Bay leaves and apple cider vinegar cannot dissolve kidney or gallstones in three days. These home remedies lack scientific backing and should not be used as a replacement for proper medical care.

claim_text: Every cell in the human body regenerates over a seven-year period. It further suggests that you become a new person every seven years.
doctor_explanation: The claim that every cell in the body regenerates in seven years is false. The adult human body consists of nearly 37 trillion cells. Each cell has its own potentially unique molecular traits. Different types of cells renew at varying rates, while some do not regenerate at all. Cells like skin cells regenerate quickly, approximately every two to four weeks, due to the continuous wear and tear they experience from the environment. Red blood cells, on the other hand, have a lifespan of about 120 days, after which they are replaced. Even bone cells undergo regeneration, but this takes around 10 years. However, some cells, such as neurons in the brain, particularly in areas like the cerebral cortex, do not regenerate once they are formed. These neurons are responsible for critical functions like memory and cognition, and they last a lifetime. A 2020 study discovered that after a brain injury in adults, cells become less mature, which might help them grow again. So, the idea that all cells are replaced every seven years is a misunderstanding of how different cells in the body function. Dr Kunal Gupta, MD, Emergency Physician at Accord Super Speciality Hospital, Faridabad, says, 'Every day, millions of skin cells renew through division, while dead cells are shed. Different types of cells have varying lifespans, except for neurons, which generally do not regenerate after birth. While the liver has the remarkable ability to regenerate, even after partial removal, most other tissues, like heart muscle cells, cannot fully repair themselves. Skin, however, has a strong capacity for regeneration. The human body contains two key types of cells: somatic cells, which make up most of the body, and stem cells, which help in the repair and renewal of tissues, though their capacity to fully regenerate organs is still limited.' Regarding exceptions to cellular regeneration: liver tissue can regenerate, but heart muscle cells (cardiomyocytes) have very limited ability to do so. When adult heart cells are damaged, they can't easily regrow, leading to scarring instead of proper healing. Brain neurons do not regenerate like skin or blood cells. Once these neurons are damaged or die, the body doesn't naturally replace them. Dr Almas Fatma, MBBS, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician from Navi Mumbai, states, 'Cell regeneration isn't as straightforward as a complete body renewal every seven years. Some cells, like skin and blood cells, are replaced regularly, but critical cells in the heart and brain don't regenerate easily. This is why damage in these areas tends to be permanent, debunking the idea of a total body reset.' The liver is an organ with regenerative abilities, but even this process does not follow a simple timeline like the seven-year rule. The liver can regenerate to a significant extent, but its ability to do so depends on various factors such as the extent of injury or damage, genetic factors, and the overall health of the individual. Liver regeneration involves complex biological processes like cell division, signalling pathways, and tissue repair. Even though the liver can regenerate, this does not apply to the entire body's cells and tissues. The idea that you become a completely new person every seven years is misleading. Although many of the body's cells do regenerate, the rates of regeneration vary drastically. Additionally, the process of regeneration doesn't erase the effects of ageing or accumulated damage. Factors such as DNA mutations, environmental stress, and cellular damage contribute to ageing. This implies that parts of the human body degrade over time rather than being fully renewed. Some cells, like neurons, stay with us for life, disproving the claim of complete renewal. Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, General Physician, Holy Mission Clinic, New Delhi, says, 'The notion that the entire body renews itself every seven years is an oversimplification. It's true that some cells, like those in the skin, regenerate frequently. But others, such as brain and heart cells, regenerate very slowly or not at all. This helps explain why injuries to organs like the heart can have long-lasting consequences.' THIP Media Take: The claim that the body fully regenerates every seven years is false. Some cells regenerate, but the rates vary depending on the cell type. Plus, certain cells, such as brain neurons, do not regenerate at all. Therefore, the body does not undergo a complete renewal every seven years, and the accumulation of cellular damage over time plays a significant role in the ageing process.

claim_text: Pfizer has released a list of dangerous side effects of its COVID-19 vaccine, including: Blood thrombosis, Acute kidney injury, Acute flaccid myelitis, Positive antisperm antibodies, Brainstem embolism, Brainstem thrombosis, Cardiac arrest (hundreds of cases), Heart failure, Cardiac ventricular thrombosis, Cardiogenic shock, Central nervous system vasculitis, Neonatal death, Deep vein thrombosis, Brainstem encephalitis, Hemorrhagic encephalitis, Frontal lobe epilepsy, Foaming at the mouth, Epileptic psychosis, Facial paralysis, Fetal distress syndrome, Gastrointestinal amyloidosis, Generalized tonic-clonic seizure, Hashimoto's encephalopathy, Hepatic vascular thrombosis, Herpes zoster reactivation, Hepatitis Immune-mediated, Interstitial lung disease, Jugular vein embolism, Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, Liver damage, Low birth weight, Multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children, Myocarditis, Neonatal seizure, Pancreatitis, Pneumonia, Stillbirth, Tachycardia, Temporal lobe epilepsy, Testicular autoimmunity, Thrombotic stroke, Type 1 diabetes mellitus, Neonatal venous thrombosis, Vertebral artery thrombosis, Pericarditis, Sudden death.
doctor_explanation: The fact-check article clarifies the critical distinction between 'side effects' and 'adverse events'. In 2022, Pfizer submitted a report of adverse events as part of its Biological License Application (BLA) to the U.S. FDA. The report compiled data from 63 countries, including the U.S., UK, Italy, Germany, and France, and contained nine pages of 'adverse events of special interest'. Pfizer clarified in the report that an accumulation of adverse event reports (AERs) does not necessarily imply causation — the reported events could be due to underlying diseases, patient history, or other medications. A side effect is a predictable reaction associated with a drug, treatment, or medical intervention, typically documented in drug information based on clinical trial observations, ranging from mild to severe. An adverse event (AE) is any unintended medical occurrence that arises during the use of a drug or treatment, regardless of a direct causal link — adverse events can be unexpected, serious, or potentially life-threatening. The claim mischaracterizes a regulatory filing of reported adverse events as a confirmed list of dangerous side effects, which is medically inaccurate. The overall safety profile of the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine remains strong, with benefits outweighing risks.

claim_text: A Facebook video showing a person performing CPR on an unconscious individual, claiming it demonstrates the correct lifesaving procedure for heart attack emergencies
doctor_explanation: What is CPR? Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is a procedure to restart a heart that has stopped beating. This condition is called cardiac arrest as the heart's electrical system stops sending signals for the heart to beat. Heartbeat can also stop in case of a heart attack. During a heart attack, blood flow to the heart gets significantly reduced due to a blocked artery. In the case of a heart attack, CPR is no use as long as the person having a heart attack is alert and breathing. Also, CPR does not work on all unconscious people with a heart attack. Is the method shown in video correct? No. We referred to the CPR steps provided by the American Red Cross Training Services and found that the person in the Facebook video is performing the wrong CPR. The fingers while giving chest compressions must be interlocked. Also, the body posture of the unconscious person must remain straight, which was not followed in the video as the unconscious individual's neck was tilting throughout the video. Also, the process does not require a handkerchief to give breaths, as shown in the video. The video also does not talk about compressions to ventilations ratio. After performing 30 chest compressions, two rescue breaths must be administered mouth to mouth, mouth to mask or through stoma, as appropriate. For children and infants, if two rescuers are performing CPR, this ratio changes to 15:2. No. Most social media videos do not give the correct picture of the process. From the Facebook video, it is evident that CPR must be given only by experienced healthcare professionals. A layman should only watch the video to understand the basic steps involved in giving CPR as well as when and why CPR should be done. Mere watching social media videos will never provide hands-on experience, which is essential to follow the correct procedure. The same has been confirmed by a research published in 2022 that informs no video presents 100% compliance with the American Heart Association guidelines. Also, there is no method to supervise and control health-related contents that allow people to post mistaken videos, which are used as learning material by many people. Doing CPR is not as easy as it looks in videos. Regular practice of CPR gives an idea of strength and ability to continue doing CPR along with an understanding of the depth needed for each chest compression. Good CPR requires an in-person class with mannequins which is monitored by a good instructor.

claim_text: Spiny Gourd or Kantola is the most powerful vegetable in Ayurveda and is 50 times more powerful and protein-rich than beef or chicken.
doctor_explanation:
Kantola, also known as Spiny Gourd or Momordica dioica, holds a place of value in Ayurvedic tradition for various health benefits. But claiming it is the 'most powerful' is an oversimplification. Ayurveda recognises the medicinal properties of a wide range of plants and vegetables, with their 'power' or efficacy depending on individual constitution (Dosha), the specific health issue being addressed, and how they are prepared and consumed. Different vegetables are prized for different properties. For instance, bitter gourd (Karela) can help in blood sugar regulation properties, while Ashwagandha acts as an adaptogen. Singling out one vegetable as universally 'most powerful' doesn't align with the holistic and context-dependent nature of Ayurvedic principles. Dr Muskan Thakur, BAMS, Ayurveda Consultant from Indore says, 'Kantola, or spine gourd, is indeed valued in Ayurveda for its lightness and ability to support digestion, especially during the monsoon season. But calling it the 'most powerful' vegetable is an exaggeration. Ayurveda does not rank foods in that way. Every vegetable has its own role based on season, body type, and balance of doshas. Kantola is good, but it's not a miracle food. A balanced diet, including a variety of seasonal vegetables, is always more important than focusing on one item alone.'

The idea of a vegetable being '50 times more powerful' than meat is not a concept usually used in nutritional science. 'Power' in terms of food is usually related to its energy density (calories) or the concentration of specific nutrients and beneficial compounds it provides. While kantola is undoubtedly nutritious, containing vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants, comparing its overall 'power' at a 50-fold magnitude against complex foods like beef or chicken is not scientifically meaningful or accurate. Meat provides a dense source of complete proteins, iron, zinc, and B vitamins, which are essential for bodily functions. Vegetables offer different, yet equally vital, nutrients like fibre, certain vitamins (like Vitamin C), and unique phytochemicals. They serve different but complementary roles in a balanced diet.

This specific part of the claim is demonstrably false based on standard nutritional composition data. Protein content is a well-defined nutritional metric that can be measured and compared accurately. Lean beef and chicken breast are widely recognised as excellent sources of high-quality protein. 100 grams of cooked chicken can give you around 25 grams of protein, while the same amount of kantola offers less than 2 grams. Comparing these figures, 30 grams of protein (from meat) is clearly not 50 times less than 2-3 grams (from kantola). In reality, beef or chicken provides significantly more protein per 100 grams than kantola. The claim reverses and massively exaggerates the actual protein content comparison between these foods. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition says, 'No, kantola is not 50 times richer in protein than beef or chicken. In fact, vegetables like kantola contain very little protein when compared to animal sources. Even though kantola is healthy and has its own benefits, like being low in calories and high in fibre, it cannot replace meat when it comes to protein content.'

claim_text: According to an Instagram post, the COVID-19 pandemic was intentionally engineered or grossly exaggerated as a pretext for a conspiracy involving governments, major pharmaceutical companies (such as Pfizer and Moderna), large financial institutions (such as BlackRock and Vanguard), and global health organisations (such as the WHO). The primary goals were allegedly to transfer trillions in wealth to elites and establish greater control over the global population.
doctor_explanation: The fact check examined multiple aspects of the claim: 1) Was the COVID-19 virus engineered based on pre-existing patents? No, this is false. The overwhelming scientific consensus, supported by extensive genomic analysis, indicates that SARS-CoV-2, the virus causing COVID-19, originated naturally, most likely through zoonotic spillover (transfer from animals to humans). Scientists have studied coronaviruses for decades, leading to patents on related viruses or vaccine technologies. However, there is no credible evidence that SARS-CoV-2 itself was engineered or patented before the outbreak. Claims of '200+ pre-pandemic patents' proving engineering are vague, unsubstantiated, and misrepresent the nature of scientific patenting. 2) Did Moderna patent mRNA vaccines to prepare for COVID-19? No. Moderna filed patents related to mRNA technology years before COVID-19, but that's common in research and not proof of a conspiracy. The company was founded in 2010 to explore mRNA as a new platform for various diseases. Patents filed in 2015 were part of general research, not specific to SARS-CoV-2. mRNA vaccine research has been ongoing for decades. Scientists began developing COVID-specific vaccines only after the virus was identified in early 2020. 3) Was the pandemic response primarily a $100 trillion wealth transfer driven by Big Pharma and finance? No, this is misleading. It is true that pharmaceutical companies like Pfizer and Moderna saw substantial revenues from their COVID-19 vaccines and treatments. The pandemic also caused massive economic disruption globally, worsening wealth inequality and benefiting certain sectors. However, characterising this complex situation solely as a planned '$100 trillion wealth transfer' orchestrated by specific entities is a significant distortion. The '$100 trillion' figure appears vastly inflated and lacks credible sourcing. Governments worldwide spent trillions, but largely on public health responses, economic support programmes (like furlough schemes), and aid to mitigate the pandemic's devastating impact, not simply funnelling money to corporations. Large investment firms like BlackRock and Vanguard do hold shares in pharmaceutical companies, as they do in many other sectors. They manage assets on behalf of clients. Claiming they 'seized control' of the pandemic response is misleading. 4) Were pandemic policies like lockdowns designed solely for control? No, this is incorrect. Public health measures such as lockdowns, mask mandates, and social distancing were implemented worldwide based on scientific advice available at the time. Their main goal was to slow the spread of a new and dangerous virus. They aimed to prevent healthcare systems from being overwhelmed. Another key aim was to reduce deaths. These steps also helped buy time to develop treatments and vaccines. While the necessity, effectiveness, and socio-economic costs of specific measures remain subjects of legitimate debate and research, attributing them purely to a desire for authoritarian 'control' dismisses the genuine public health emergency faced globally. 5) Did NIH funding and DARPA's mRNA interest indicate a link to bioweapons? No, this is false. It's documented that the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) has funded virology research globally, including collaborations in Wuhan studying coronaviruses. This is standard practice to understand and prepare for potential infectious disease threats. The term 'gain-of-function' research is often misused. While some NIH-funded research involved modifying viruses, there is no credible evidence linking this funding directly to the creation or release of SARS-CoV-2. Similarly, DARPA explored mRNA technology in the context of rapid vaccine development and medical countermeasures for pandemic preparedness – a defensive, not offensive application. Linking these research streams to suggest a bioweapon conspiracy is speculative and not supported by available evidence. THIP Media Take: The claim that COVID-19 was a planned wealth transfer, not a real pandemic is false. It mixes unrelated facts, stretches timelines, and misrepresents the roles of scientific and public health institutions. While financial inequalities deepened during the pandemic, the virus and its impact were very real. COVID-19 killed millions, disrupted economies, and led to unprecedented public health challenges—not a pre-planned wealth grab.

claim_text: Consuming a mixture of black pepper, nigella seeds, fenugreek seeds, and jamun seed powder on an empty stomach each morning can cure any type of diabetes, regardless of severity, within 3 weeks.
doctor_explanation: Diabetes is a chronic condition that occurs when the body cannot effectively manage blood glucose levels. Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition where the body's immune system attacks insulin-producing cells in the pancreas, leading to an insulin deficiency. Type 2 diabetes, the more common form, is characterised by insulin resistance. Here, the body's cells do not respond properly to insulin, often combined with an eventual insulin deficiency. Both types need careful management, involving medication, lifestyle changes, and in the case of Type 1, insulin therapy. Diabetes is a long-term health issue, and diet and lifestyle changes can significantly improve management. But still, there is currently no cure for either Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes. Black pepper, nigella seeds, fenugreek seeds, and jamun seed powder have all been studied for their potential health benefits including their effects on blood sugar levels. However, this mixture cannot cure diabetes in 3 weeks. Diabetes is a complex and chronic condition that requires long-term management. The claim that this mixture can cure diabetes overlooks the need for a comprehensive approach, including medication, lifestyle changes, and regular monitoring. Currently, no cure exists for Type 1 diabetes, and while Type 2 diabetes can often be managed with lifestyle adjustments and medication, it is still not curable. Relying on such claims can be dangerous, as it might lead people to neglect proven treatments, likely worsening their condition. Dietician Kamana Chauhan says, "When it comes to diabetes, there's no magic bullet, despite what some claims might suggest. As a dietician, I've seen how easy it is to get caught up in the promise of quick fixes, but managing diabetes is a marathon, not a sprint. Ingredients like fenugreek and jamun seed powder can support blood sugar control, but they aren't a cure-all. True diabetes management requires a thoughtful balance of medical care, healthy eating, and regular exercise. Always have a discussion with your dietician or doctor before changing your routine – it's about finding what works best for you." Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, states, "Dealing with diabetes can be tough, and it's natural to look for easy solutions. But, I want to make it clear that no food or mixture can cure diabetes. Ingredients like fenugreek and jamun seed powder might help keep blood sugar in check, but they can't take the place of the treatments your doctor recommends. Managing diabetes well means sticking to your medication, eating a balanced diet, and staying active. Before trying anything new, it's always best to check in with your dietician or physician." Following unverified health advice poses several risks. Discontinuing prescribed diabetes medication or altering a treatment plan without consulting a healthcare provider can lead to uncontrolled blood sugar levels, increasing risk of serious complications such as heart disease, nerve damage, and kidney problems. While the ingredients in this mixture are generally safe in moderation, they can interact with medications or cause side effects. For instance, fenugreek can cause digestive issues, and jamun seeds might lower blood sugar levels excessively if combined with other anti-diabetic medications.

claim_text: Eating flaxseeds can enhance breast size by boosting oestrogen levels
doctor_explanation: Does flaxseed increase breast size? No, flaxseed does not increase breast size. While flaxseeds are often associated with hormonal health due to their lignan content (plant compounds with weak estrogen-like effects), they cannot increase breast size. These compounds, known as phytoestrogens, mimic estrogen in a very mild way, but their impact is far too small to cause noticeable changes in breast tissue. A case study was studied in 2020 when a 70-year-old male with hyperlipidaemia began consuming a tablespoon of flaxseed oil daily. After three months, he experienced swelling and pain in his left breast. An ultrasound detected a tumour in the left mammary gland, but a biopsy confirmed gynecomastia, showing ductal hyperplasia without malignancy. The breast tissue was oestrogen receptor-positive, prompting a discussion about the potential impact of phytoestrogens. Flaxseeds are primarily valued for their high fibre, omega-3 fatty acids, and antioxidant content. Any hormonal effects they may have are more about supporting overall balance than creating dramatic physical changes. Additionally, the size of breasts depends on genetics, body weight, hormonal levels, and life stages, not the consumption of a particular food. Why do some people believe flaxseed increases breast size? Dr. Mohit Sandhu, BAMS, CAD, CAC, PGDAKS, Founder of the Association for Ayurvedic Palpative Pain Medicine, Gurgaon, says, 'The belief likely stems from misunderstandings about phytoestrogens.' Flaxseeds contain a type of phytoestrogen that can interact with oestrogen receptors in the body. This has led to the misconception that eating flaxseeds might mimic the effects of oestrogen and lead to breast enlargement. However, Studies have shown that phytoestrogens may help balance oestrogen levels—reducing its effects when levels are too high or slightly supporting them when they are low. This balancing act does not result in an increase in breast tissue growth. Are there foods that can naturally increase breast size? No single food can naturally increase breast size. Breast size is known by a combination of genetics, hormonal levels, and overall body fat composition. While a balanced diet can support hormonal health, no specific food, including flaxseeds, directly influences breast size. The idea of 'breast-enhancing foods' is often used as a marketing tactic and lacks scientific backing. Eating nutrient-rich foods like flaxseeds, soy, or nuts might improve overall health, but they won't cause noticeable growth in breast tissue. Dr. Kashyap Dakshini, a General Physician in Mumbai, explains, 'For years, various devices, diets, smoothies, creams, and lotions have been promoted as breast enhancement solutions. However, scientific research has shown that none of these methods, exercises, or quick fixes can actually enlarge the breasts. While exercises can strengthen and tone the muscles supporting the breasts, they do not significantly affect breast size.' Can flaxseed improve hormonal health without changing breast size? Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, explains, 'Yes, flaxseed can support hormonal health.' They may play a role in regulating hormones. They can help stabilise oestrogen levels, particularly in postmenopausal women. Additionally, the high fibre content in flaxseeds supports gut health, which is essential for efficient hormone metabolism. Regular consumption of flaxseeds can help manage hormonal imbalances, reduce inflammation, and support heart health, but these benefits do not translate into changes in breast size. What should you focus on for better breast health? Prioritise overall wellness, not myths about specific foods. Breast health is best supported by maintaining a balanced diet, engaging in regular physical activity, managing stress, and having routine medical check-ups. Foods like flaxseeds can be a part of healthy diet, but they cannot be magical solutions for breast size or appearance. Instead of chasing unproven remedies, focus on a nutrient-rich diet that includes a variety of whole grains, vegetables, fruits, lean proteins, and healthy fats. This approach supports overall health, including hormonal balance, which is far more important than altering physical features.

claim_text: In CANCER treatment, SODIUM BICARBONATE is the PERFECT MEDICINE.
doctor_explanation: No. There are lot of discussions on the effect of alkaline food and water on body including its ability to treat cancer. However, none has been proven medically. The blood maintains a stable pH of 7.4. This makes it slightly alkaline. Diet is not known to alter pH of the blood. The confusion arises from the fact that cancer cells alter the environment around them to make it acidic. This fact has given rise to multiple theories about alkaline treatments. However, there is no conclusive evidence of alkaline diet being able to change acidic environment around cancer cells. No. There is still no conclusive evidence regarding this. The theory arises from the fact that some cancer cells and tumours learn to thrive without oxygen – a common requirement of all cells in human body. Many researchers believe that flooding the body with extra oxygen will make the cancer cells die. So far, there is no medical evidence for this theory. A recent research evidence shows that giving high dosage of oxygen to a person triggers his immune system against tumours. However, the study was done on mice and oxygen was introduced through respiratory system. Though the study paves way for further research, it still doesn't prove a total cure for all types of cancer. We asked Dr. Sarthak Moharir, Radiation Oncologist whether excess oxygen in body kill cancer cells. To this, he said "High pressure oxygen is used as a therapeutic agent to cure certain side effects of radiation. This is called Hyperbaric Oxygen therapy. But there is no proof that excess oxygen will kill cancer cells. On the contrary, inhaling pure oxygen can depress the respiratory centres of the brain to prevent normal functioning." No. There is no evidence to suggest that baking soda or bicarbonate can cure cancer. There is some evidence that bicarbonate can slow down the growth of cancer cells. A research done in 2009 showed that when bicarbonate (baking soda) is directly injected into a mice, it reduced the pH of the tumour cells and inhibited the growth of metastatic breast cancer. This is not equal to a complete cure of cancer. At the end of research, researchers concluded, "...the dramatic effect of bicarbonate therapy on the formation of breast cancer metastases in this model system warrants further investigation." But this experiment has not yet been replicated on humans and is not an approved medical practice for cancer treatment. We asked Dr Moharir why this study was not replicated on humans. In response, he explained "Injecting sodium bicarbonate in the body will cause serious side effects in the form of metabolic alkalosis. There is no proof that it kills cancer cells". THIP Media Take: Cancer treatment is a highly researched area in medical science. However, so far, alkaline therapy, oxygen therapy or bicarbonate therapy have not been conclusively proven to be effective therapy.

claim_text: A Facebook post titled '4 powerful foods that help control blood pressure naturally' asserts that pomegranate, beetroot, black raisins, and flaxseeds (particularly in powdered form) are effective blood pressure-lowering foods that can reverse high blood pressure naturally.
doctor_explanation:
High blood pressure (hypertension) is a prevalent medical condition where blood pressure against arterial walls remains persistently elevated. Often referred to as the 'silent killer,' hypertension is linked to both structural and functional alterations in blood vessels due to its early asymptomatic presentation. Undiagnosed moderately high blood pressure can shorten life expectancy by accelerating vascular damage and compromising organ perfusion. The WHO states that uncontrolled hypertension plays a major role in heart failure, myocardial infarction, stroke, and chronic renal disease, requiring evidence-based medication, lifestyle changes, and early intervention.

Research on flaxseeds shows potential benefits for lowering high blood pressure due to their high levels of dietary fibre, alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), and lignans, which have vascular-protective and anti-inflammatory attributes. Studies show flaxseed consumption may slightly decrease both systolic and diastolic blood pressures in some patients with hypertension by enhancing endothelial function, reducing arterial stiffness, and modifying lipid profiles. However, these effects are not universal and depend on dosage, duration, and individual health status.

CRITICAL: Flax seeds should NOT be considered as a substitute for evidence-based blood pressure medication. Hypertension is a multifaceted illness requiring all-encompassing care. Without medical supervision, relying on unproven home cures like flax seeds can be risky—it may delay timely intervention and contribute to the condition's gradual progression, resulting in serious complications.

Regarding regular consumption: While flax seeds can help enhance lipid profiles, support cardiovascular health, improve glycaemic control, and facilitate digestion, prolonged consumption in excess can cause bloating, diarrhoea, and gastrointestinal distress due to high fibre content. Due to phytoestrogenic qualities, people with hormone-sensitive conditions should use them cautiously. Those using prescribed blood thinners may experience interactions.

Diet cannot replace evidence-based medication. While diet is vital in managing cardiovascular conditions, hypertension requires a multimodal approach combining lifestyle and pharmaceutical therapy. The DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet has demonstrated improvements in lowering blood pressure but is not sufficient for dropping blood pressure to healthy ranges alone. Medical practitioners recommend antihypertensive medications (ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, thiazide diuretics, and beta-blockers) when lifestyle modifications are insufficient.

Dr. Almas Fatma advises the most effective ways to regulate blood pressure are: consume a nutritious diet, be physically active, limit salt intake, and manage stress. Doctors may also recommend medication in some situations to maintain blood pressure within acceptable limits.

Dr. Ubaid ur Rahman explains that lowering blood pressure takes time and requires both medical assistance and healthy lifestyle choices. Reducing alcohol consumption, quitting smoking, increasing physical activity, and consuming a diet high in fruits, vegetables, and low-fat foods are crucial support strategies. Even if some individuals require medication, lifestyle modifications are always the cornerstone of treatment.

claim_text: Eating almonds reduces belly fat
doctor_explanation: Belly fat is also called visceral fat. It is the fat around your belly organs like the liver, pancreas, and intestines. Belly fat is not the same as the fat under your skin. Having too much belly fat can cause health problems like heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers. Almonds can be a beneficial part of a healthy diet when consumed in moderation. They are rich in nutrients like vitamin E, fiber, and protein, and they can contribute to a feeling of fullness due to their protein and fiber content. Dr Sujata Chakravarti, Consultant-General Medicine, Hiranandani Hospital, Vashi-A Fortis Network Hospital, says, "Almonds are healthy because they are high in protein and fats. Also, almonds provide small amounts of Iron, Calcium, Phosphorus, Vitamin A, B Complex, and E". The combination of protein and fiber in almonds can enhance satiety, reducing hunger and potentially contributing to a sense of fullness. This may aid in managing overall calorie intake, and supporting weight management goals. A study further suggests that incorporating almonds into a balanced diet may assist in weight management due to their nutrient density and ability to promote satiety. However, it is crucial to note that this effect is not specifically targeted at reducing belly fat but rather contributes to overall weight control. Not exactly. Almonds are a nutritious food and can be part of a healthy diet. But claims of them directly reducing belly fat should be approached with caution. While they can play a role in overall health and weight management, relying solely on almonds for weight loss is not recommended. The concept of spot reduction, particularly targeting belly fat through the consumption of a specific food, lacks substantial evidence. Weight management and reduction of belly fat are multifaceted and require a holistic approach rather than relying on the effects of a single food item. Dt. Priyanka concludes, "To successfully lose fat, it requires a comprehensive approach. Simply put, you must first identify the underlying causes of weight gain, such as inflammation, leaky gut, hormone imbalances, toxins, low metabolism, or the intake of medications such as steroids. Once you have determined the root cause, you can then make the necessary adjustments to your diet and lifestyle to effectively lose fat." Almonds might not be helpful in reducing fat due to certain medical conditions. Excessive consumption can lead to an increase in calorie intake, potentially hindering weight management goals. According to the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, one ounce of almonds, which is equal to 20–24 whole almonds, contains about 165 calories. Over-consumption of almonds can be harmful and cause toxicity. As almonds are rich in fibre, overconsumption can lead to gastrointestinal issues, such as constipation (if not taken with enough water). It can also interfere with the absorption of other minerals, such as calcium, magnesium, etc. Other harmful effects include weight gain, Vitamin E overdose (rarely), cause kidney stones and rarely, can cause cyanide poisoning. Also, even though it is rare, few people also suffer from almond allergy. Dietician Kamna Chauhan states, "Consuming anything in excess leads to the risk of diseases. Almonds are healthy nuts and have many health benefits, but it also has lots of side effects if eaten in large quantities. So before grabbing almonds from the jar, we should know how much to eat. Eating too many almonds leads to many side effects such as constipation and allergy, as almonds contain a protein called Amandine, which is an allergen. It can also make people gain weight". Almond contain vitamin E and excess vitamin E interferes with blood coagulation to cause hemorrhage. Moreover, almonds also reduces nutrient absorption in the body, and can lead to kidney stones. Dr Swati Dave, Phd in Food and Nutrition adds, "Weight loss misinformation on the internet is akin to a virus, spreading quick fixes and false claims through captivating video captions. Deceptive information often promises easy solutions, promoting unrealistic expectations. Such misleading content can lead individuals to adopt ineffective or even harmful practices, hindering their pursuit of sustainable and healthy weight loss." Dietician Harita informs about common weight loss misinformation including: 1) You need to follow gluten free diet if you want to lose weight, 2) Cut off fat totally to get quick weight loss, 3) Fad diet is best for weight loss, 4) 7 days Mono diet can help to lose more fast, 5) Supplements can help you lose weight, 6) Carbs make you fat, 7) Eating breakfast is necessary to lose weight, 8) Go for high protein diet if want to lose fast, 9) Cut Out all sugar, 10) Artificial sweeteners are healthy, 11) Cut off with social life if you are on diet, 12) Lukewarm drinks for weight loss and many more.

claim_text: An Instagram video suggests that moringa seeds are highly effective in managing diabetes. It recommends that people eat three seeds during the day and three seeds at night. One can either crush or boil and strain, and then consume the drink on an empty stomach. It also refers to the moringa tree as the 'tree of life' due to its numerous health benefits.
doctor_explanation: There is scientific evidence supporting the use of moringa seeds for diabetes management, but it is essential to understand the context and limitations of this evidence. Moringa seeds cannot replace conventional diabetes treatments. A 2020 study says Moringa reduces blood glucose levels, but the evidence is not strong enough to recommend it as a primary treatment for diabetes. Moringa seeds help lower blood sugar levels and provide antioxidant benefits, making them a useful supplement for managing diabetes. However, the claim that the seeds are one of the best remedies for diabetes is an overstatement. They should be used alongside conventional treatments like medication, diet, and exercise. They are not a cure and should not replace prescribed diabetes management plans. Always consult with healthcare professionals before making changes to your regimen, especially when you are diabetic. Dr Ayush Chandra, Consultant Diabetologist and Founder of Nivaran Health, Delhi NCR, states, 'Moringa, also known as drumsticks, is thought to help reduce fasting blood sugar levels, enhance insulin sensitivity, and lower glycemic response. However, it should only be used as a supplement. The main treatments for diabetes include medication, dietary changes, lifestyle adjustments, and glucose monitoring. Be aware of potential side effects and consult a doctor about drug interactions, stomach issues, allergies, liver problems, and pregnancy-related concerns.' Dr Swati Dave, PhD Food and Nutrition, says, 'Moringa leaves and pods show potential in managing diabetes by lowering blood sugar levels and providing antioxidant benefits. It is important to ensure the seeds' quality and consult with a doctor to confirm the appropriate quantity for use. However, studies on humans are still inconclusive, and we need more research to confirm their effectiveness. It's also necessary to use moringa seeds as a supplement to conventional treatments, not a replacement. Always consult your physician before adding moringa seeds to your diabetes management plan to ensure safety and proper use.' During our research we found a detailed scientific review from 2019. The review investigates moringa oleifera (MO) as an antidiabetic agent, summarising animal and human studies on its effects on glycaemia and insulin. Animal studies show significant reductions in blood glucose across various MO extracts, though we need more long-term studies. Human studies yield mixed results, with significant glycaemia reduction in only two out of six studies. We still need standardised methodologies and further research into moringa's effects on insulin and other glucose metabolism parameters. Moringa extract is generally safe, but taste acceptability and comparative efficacy of different tree parts require more investigation. Moringa seeds are generally safe for most people, but there are some potential side effects and allergy risks to be aware of. If you're considering moringa seeds for diabetes management, start with small amounts and gradually increase if no side effects occur. Use them to supplement a balanced diet, regular exercise, and prescribed medications—not as a substitute. Regularly monitor your blood sugar levels and adjust your intake as needed, keeping your healthcare provider updated. Ensure the seeds are of good quality and confirm the right dosage with a diabetologist. Moringa seeds show potential in helping manage diabetes due to their hypoglycemic and antioxidant properties. However, calling them the 'best remedy' is an overstatement. They can be a helpful addition to a comprehensive diabetes management plan but should not replace conventional treatments. The claim that moringa seeds are one of the best remedies for diabetes is mostly false due to the lack of conclusive evidence. Their benefits are real but should be integrated into a broader, medically-supervised treatment strategy.

claim_text: Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered the destruction of all COVID vaccines in Russia
doctor_explanation: Not exactly. No published evidence confirms that Putin has made such an order. We found no press release or any other official document on the Russian government or state-owned TASS news agency.
